'''''Lepidozamia peroffskyana''''' is a [[Palm (plant)|palm]]-like [[cycad]] in the family [[Zamiaceae]]. It is [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern Australia, in [[Queensland]] and [[New South Wales]].  The species is named after [[Vasily Alekseevich Perovsky|Count Peroffsky]] (1794-1857), benefactor of the [[St. Petersburg Botanical Garden]].

==Description==
[[image:Lepidozamia Peroffskyana leaf.jpg|thumb|left|Leaf detail.]]
''Lepidozamia peroffskyana'' is slow-growing, low maintenance, long-lived [[cycad]] that makes a good feature plant in semi-shaded positions or in a container. It grows up to seven metres tall but more usually reaches about four metres. The [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]] is up to eighty centimetres in diameter and is covered by the persistent remains of leaf bases forming an interesting texture. The [[Crown (botany)|crown]] develops from numerous leaves up to three metres long, each bearing about two hundred narrow, glossy, dark green leaflets, somewhat lax, spreading and softly [[coriaceous]]. Each has seven to thirteen parallel veins which helps to distinguish this species from other members of the genus.<ref name="CP">{{Cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/cycadpg?taxname=Lepidozamia+peroffskyana |title=The Cycad Pages |access-date=3 December 2010 |archive-date=18 July 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050718230905/http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/cycadpg?taxname=Lepidozamia+peroffskyana }}</ref> The plant produces a rosette of [[Frond|fronds]] each year, there being six rosettes at any given time, stacked one above the other. As the newest matures, the lowest one dies back.<ref>{{cite book |last=Butt |title=An Introduction to the Zamiaceae in Australia |date=1991 |publisher=Palm and Cycad Societies of Australia |isbn=0-9587931-5-8 |location=Milton, Queensland |page=13}}</ref> The cylindrical cones are some of the largest of all cycad cones, rivalled only by ''[[Encephalartos transvenosus]]''.<ref name="DJ">Jones, David L. ''Cycads of the World''. (1993) Reed Books.</ref> The male cones can reach seventy five centimetres long and the female cones ninety centimetres, weighing up to forty five kilograms.<ref name="DJ"/> The seeds are large and numerous and have red [[sarcotesta]].<ref name="CP"/> 

All parts of the plant, especially the seeds, are toxic to both livestock and humans. If ingested, the seeds can cause severe gastrointestinal irritation and abdominal cramps, vomiting and nausea, diarrhea, and potentially also liver damage and muscular paralysis.<ref name="childrens_health_qld">[https://www.childrens.health.qld.gov.au/poisonous-plant-burrawang-palm-lepidozamia-peroffskyana/ Children's Health Queensland Hospital and Health Service: Burrawang palm (Lepidozamia peroffskyana)]</ref>

==Reproductive biology==
[[File:Lepidozamia peroffskyana cone.jpg|thumb|left|''L. peroffskyana'' cone]]The [[pollen]] of this cycad is not airborne. Typically, the pollen is transported by a host-specific insect from male to female cones when they are receptive.<ref name="Donaldson1997">{{cite journal |last1=Donaldson |first1=J. S. |title=Is there a floral parasite mutualism in cycad pollination? The pollination biology of ''Encephalartos villosus'' |journal=American Journal of Botany |date=1997 |volume=84 |pages=1398–1406|doi=10.2307/2446138 |jstor=2446138 }}</ref> Pollen of ''L. peroffskyana'' is carried by the ''[[Tranes]]'' group [[Weevil|weevils]]. The weevil's life-cycle occurs in the male cones, but many individuals visit female cones during their lives, covered in pollen. The plant exudes a scent to attract the weevils to the reproductive cones. Weevils gather at the male cones as they are about to open and release pollen. The male cones supply pollen and biomaterial so that the weevils have sites for oviposition as well as food as their activity destroys the cones.<ref name="Hall_et_al2004">{{cite journal |last1=Hall |first1=John A. |last2=Walter |first2=Gimme H. |last3=Bergstrom |first3=Dana M. |last4=Machin |first4=Peter |title=Pollination ecology of the Australian cycad Lepidozamia peroffskyana (Zamiaceae) |journal=Australian Journal of Botany |date=2004 |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=333–343 |doi=10.1071/BT03159 |url=https://www.publish.csiro.au/bt/pdf/bt03159#:~:text=The%20cycad%20L.,both%20male%20and%20female%20cones.}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
This species is found in southeastern [[Queensland]] and northeastern [[New South Wales]], occurring between [[Gympie]], north of [[Brisbane]] and the [[Manning River]] near [[Forster, New South Wales|Forster]]. It grows in scattered small communities in wet [[sclerophyll]] forests or on [[rainforest]] margins, usually on steep slopes from sea level up to about 1,000 metres.<ref name="iucn status 14 November 2021" />
